neutral_facts.value: The prosecution case was that on the fateful day, accused persons equipped with deadly weapons reached the spot of occurrence and started inflicting injuries on the deceased and others. Thereafter, the accused persons fled away. The police van reached the spot and removed the deceased to the hospital where he was declared dead. A Parcha Bayan was lodged by a witness who was the brother of the deceased. The prosecution examined 33 witnesses and presented evidence of injuries found on the deceased's body. The trial court accepted the prosecution case and convicted the accused under Sections 148, 201, and 302 of the IPC. The High Court set aside the conviction under Sections 148 and 201 but upheld the conviction under Section 302. The Supreme Court, however, found that the evidence of the brother of the deceased, who was a highly interested witness, was not reliable. The evidence of an independent witness, a police constable, and others contradicted the presence of the brother of the deceased at the scene of the offense, leading to the conclusion that the prosecution's case was based on unreliable evidence.

quotes.text: The trial court accepted the prosecution case and convicted the appellants under Sections 148, 201 and 302 IPC. On appeal, High Court set aside conviction under Sections 148 and 201. It however upheld conviction under Section 302 IPC. Hence the present appeal.

Allowing the appeal, the Court HELD: 1.1. The concurrent findings of facts are not usually interfered with in exercise of jurisdiction under Article 136 of the Constitution of India by re-appreciation of the evidence unless it is clearly established that the courts below altogether ignored vital piece of evidence and rested their conclusion placing reliance on the evidence which cannot be accepted on the face of it.

prosecution_argument.value: The prosecution argued that the accused persons equipped with deadly weapons reached the scene of occurrence and inflicted injuries on the deceased and others, leading to the deceased's death. The case was based on the Parcha Bayan lodged by PW-5, and the trial court accepted the prosecution's case.

quotes.text: The prosecution case is as follows : On May 25, 1999 at about 1.00 p.m., Chuttu @ Nizamuddin (PW-5) lodged a Parcha Bayan (Ex.P-12) before the Police Sub-Inspector of Kotwali, Tonk inter-alia stating that at about 12.30 in the noon he along with Saleem (PW-7) and Noor (PW-13) were getting a truck repaired at Rajasthan Tyrewala near Roadways Depot, Tonk. One Mohamaad Deen @ Mulla (deceased) came at the shop of Ayub Bhai (PW-6). All of a sudden about 10-12 persons equipped with deadly weapons such as gupties, swords, knives and gandasas came there and surrounded the deceased.

defence_argument.value: The defence argued that the incident took place out of acute enmity and that the evidence of highly interested eye-witnesses should be rejected as there is a likelihood of implicating innocent persons. The defence also highlighted the presence of independent witnesses whose evidence contradicted the prosecution's case.

quotes.text: The defence argued that the incident took place out of acute enmity. The evidence of highly interested eye-witness should be rejected as there is likelihood of implicating some innocent persons.

Shri Amarender Sharan, learned senior counsel, inter-alia, submitted that the presence of alleged eye-witnesses at the scene of offence is highly doubtful and no reliance can be placed on their evidence.

legal_principle_applied.value: The Supreme Court applied the principle that concurrent findings of facts are not usually interfered with by the court under Article 136 of the Constitution of India unless it is clearly established that the courts below altogether ignored vital piece of evidence and rested their conclusion on evidence that cannot be accepted on the face of it.

quotes.text: Concurrent findings of facts are not usually interfered with in exercise of jurisdiction under Article 136 of the Constitution of India by re-appreciation of the evidence unless it is clearly established that courts below altogether ignored vital piece of evidence and rested their conclusion placing reliance on the evidence which could not be accepted on the face of it.
